passage: Sunday. Pradeep Dada told Siddharth about his own elder brother, a soldier who held a mountain post through a snowstorm. Siddharth forgot to blink. "Weren't you scared for him?" "Every day." Wednesday. Siddharth had broken the classroom window with a ball, and the others had run off. His stomach knotted, but he thought of the soldier and walked to the teacher's table to say it was him. Saturday. He joined Dada at the colony clean-up, dragging a sack of leaves. "Soldiers keep the border," he said. "Somebody has to keep the colony."

qa.a: He broke the classroom window with a ball.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling while Dada told the soldier's story?
qa.a: Awe: he forgot to blink and asked whether Dada was scared for his brother.

qa.q: How did Siddharth turn his admiration into action?
qa.a: He told the teacher the truth about the window and joined the colony clean-up.

qa.q: How might Pradeep Dada feel seeing Siddharth at the clean-up?
qa.a: Probably proud and moved, since the story about his brother seems to have reached his grandson.

grounding: Illustrates a child awed by a soldier's story who expresses admiration through honesty and helping the community.

passage: On the class trip to the small town museum, the guide stopped at a faded photo of a young woman in a white sari. 'This is Sarala Bai, from right here in our town,' she said. 'When she was only sixteen, she taught poor children to read in secret at night, even when the police came looking. She said a free country needs people who can read.' Gopika stared at the photo. Sixteen. Only six years older than her. Her skin tingled all over. 'I could never be that brave,' she whispered to Irfan. 'Maybe not police-brave,' Irfan said. 'But you could teach reading.' That evening, Gopika took out her old storybooks and sat on the steps with the watchman's little daughter. They read one page together. It felt like a tiny piece of the photo.

qa.q: How old was Sarala Bai when she taught children in secret?
How did Gopika feel looking at the photo?
qa.a: Awed and inspired; her skin tingled all over, even though she doubted she could be that brave.

qa.q: How did Gopika turn her admiration into action?
qa.a: She read a storybook with the watchman's little daughter, serving in a small way.

qa.q: How did Irfan see Gopika's worry about not being brave?
qa.a: He thought she could still help in her own way, like teaching reading.

grounding: On a museum trip a girl is awed by a local freedom fighter's story and serves in a small way by teaching a child to read.

passage:
Saturday. Chaitanya's uncle, a soldier home on leave from a post high in the mountains, told them about the snow: how he and his friends dug out a stranded bus of pilgrims in the freezing night, passing every blanket they had to the children. Chaitanya sat with his mouth open. A shiver of awe stayed with him all through dinner.
Sunday. Chaitanya kept thinking about it. 'I want to be brave like Chachu,' he told his sister Aditi. 'You're ten,' she said. 'You can't dig out buses.' 'Then what can I do?'
Wednesday. At school, Chaitanya signed up to be the morning helper for the Class 1 children at the gate, carrying bags for the smallest ones. It wasn't snow. But it felt like his own small post.

qa.q: What did Chachu and his friends dig out?
How did Chaitanya feel listening to Chachu's story?
qa.a: Full of awe; a shiver stayed with him all through dinner.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya turn awe into service?
qa.a: He became the morning helper for Class 1 children at the gate, carrying bags for the smallest ones.

qa.q: How did Aditi respond to Chaitanya wanting to be brave?
qa.a: Practically; she reminded him he was ten and couldn't dig out buses, which made him look for something he could do.

grounding: Over several days a boy awed by his soldier uncle's story finds a small way to serve at school.
